body:
The extent of the Mauryan Empire

The Mauryan Empire was one of the largest political formations of ancient India. Its authority extended from the north-western frontier, including regions of present-day Afghanistan and Baluchistan, across much of northern and central India and into substantial parts of the Deccan.

Under Ashoka, the conquest of Kalinga brought an important region of the eastern coast under Mauryan control.

However, the Mauryan Empire did not include the entire Indian subcontinent. The far south contained independent political formations, including the Cholas and Pandyas, which Ashoka's inscriptions mention separately.

The geographical extent of an empire must also be distinguished from the intensity of its administration. A large territory could be politically subject to the emperor without being governed everywhere through identical arrangements.

The 5 major political centres

NCERT identifies 5 major political centres associated with Mauryan administration: the imperial capital Pataliputra and the provincial centres Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri.

Political centreBroad locationImportance
PataliputraPresent-day Patna, BiharImperial capital and centre of direct royal administration
TaxilaNorth-west, present-day PakistanGateway towards the north-west and Central Asia
UjjayiniPresent-day Ujjain, Madhya PradeshImportant centre on routes connecting northern and southern India
TosaliKalinga region, present-day OdishaEastern provincial administrative centre
SuvarnagiriSouthern Deccan, associated with present-day KarnatakaSouthern political centre, possibly connected with access to gold resources

Suvarnagiri is traditionally associated with the southern Deccan and may have been important because of nearby gold resources. Its precise identification and the exact geographical limits of its administration should not be stated with unnecessary certainty.

Why these centres were important

Pataliputra and the Gangetic heartland

Pataliputra was the imperial capital. The densely settled agricultural region around it provided substantial revenue and supported direct administration by officials acting under the emperor.

Taxila and the north-west

Taxila occupied an important position on routes connecting the Gangetic region with north-western India and Central Asia. Control over this centre helped the Mauryas maintain communication with their north-western territories and oversee movement along important trade corridors.

Ujjayini and north-south communication

Ujjayini stood on an important route between northern and southern India. It helped connect the Gangetic heartland with western and central India and routes extending into the Deccan.

Tosali and Kalinga

Tosali was associated with the eastern region of Kalinga. Its importance increased in the context of Mauryan authority over this coastal territory.

Suvarnagiri and the southern territories

Suvarnagiri served as a major southern administrative centre. Its position helped link Mauryan authority with the resource-rich regions of the Deccan.

Taxila was associated with the north-western gateway, while Ujjayini was associated with routes from northern to southern India. These geographical functions should not be interchanged.

How the empire was connected

A geographically extensive empire could function only if its political centres maintained communication with one another.

Two types of routes were particularly important:

  • Land routes: Roads and established trade corridors carried officials, soldiers, messengers, merchants and supplies between major settlements.
  • River routes: Navigable rivers supported the transport of goods and facilitated communication, particularly in the Gangetic plains.

Long journeys required arrangements for food, protection and transportation. Communication between Pataliputra and distant provinces could take several weeks or even months.

The Mauryas therefore needed to control important roads, river crossings and strategic centres, rather than relying on the physical presence of the emperor throughout the empire.

Political control was not equally strong everywhere

Administrative control was strongest near Pataliputra and major provincial centres. It was generally less direct in remote territories, forests and areas between these centres.

Some forest communities retained considerable independence while supplying goods such as timber, elephants, honey and wax. Provincial authorities probably also accommodated some local customs and arrangements.

The southern frontier

Ashoka's inscriptions mention southern political groups such as the Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputras and Keralaputras, as well as Tamraparni, generally associated with Sri Lanka.

The references distinguish neighbouring territories from regions under direct Mauryan rule. Diplomatic or moral influence beyond imperial boundaries should not be confused with political annexation.

Prelims focus

  • Pataliputra was the imperial capital.
  • Taxila was the gateway towards the north-west.
  • Ujjayini was associated with north-south trade routes.
  • Tosali was associated with Kalinga.
  • Suvarnagiri was a southern provincial centre.
  • Trap: The Cholas and Pandyas were not simply Mauryan provinces because they appear in Ashoka's inscriptions.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed pp. 76–78; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, section 3.2, Administering the Empire, printed pp. 32–34; Ashoka, Major Rock Edicts II and XIII, English translation by S. Dhammika, Livius.org, Ashoka's Rock Edicts, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Within Mauryan authority, control was strongest around Pataliputra, regional at Taxila and Ujjayini, and less direct in remote and forest regions.
pictures.caption: Different regions of the Mauryan Empire experienced different degrees of direct administration.

title: Mauryan Imperial Geography: Political Centres, Frontiers and Communication Routes

body:
The challenge of governing a large empire

The Mauryan rulers controlled a much larger territory than the earlier kings of individual mahajanapadas. They therefore needed administrative arrangements capable of collecting revenue, maintaining order, communicating instructions and protecting important regions.

These functions were connected. Revenue paid for officials and soldiers; officials supervised local affairs; communication routes enabled instructions and supplies to move; and military forces protected political authority.

Direct administration and provincial government

Administration around Pataliputra

The area around the imperial capital was under relatively direct royal control. Officials collected taxes, supervised economic activities and enforced the ruler's instructions.

The emperor exercised authority with the assistance of senior ministers, members of the royal family and other officials. Some officials received salaries for their service.

Administration in the provinces

Distant regions were governed through provincial centres. Members of the royal family, including princes, were often appointed to important provincial responsibilities.

Provincial administration allowed imperial authority to operate away from Pataliputra. Nevertheless, local customs and existing arrangements could continue. This is why Mauryan administration should not be imagined as completely identical in every region.

Messengers and intelligence

Messengers carried instructions and information between the capital and other regions. Spies and other agents helped rulers obtain information about officials and conditions within the empire.

These arrangements were particularly valuable because distance made direct supervision difficult.

Taxes and tribute

The Mauryan government required substantial resources for the army, officials and administrative establishments.

Taxes could be collected from cultivators, herders, artisans and traders. Their contributions supported the continuing expenses of government.

It is important to distinguish tax from tribute.

FeatureTaxTribute
NatureRegularly collected revenue obligationContribution collected or received when possible
Typical contextTerritories under regular administrationAreas with less direct or more variable control
Possible formAgricultural produce, goods or other assessed contributionsValuable products, materials or other contributions
Administrative significanceSupports continuing state expenditureProvides resources without necessarily requiring identical regular taxation

For example, some forest communities may have supplied elephants, timber, honey or wax. Such contributions did not necessarily imply that these communities were governed through the same arrangements as farmers living near Pataliputra.

Taxation implies a regular revenue obligation. Tribute may be occasional and depends on the relationship between the contributor and the political authority.

Military organisation

The army protected the empire against external threats, supported political authority within its territories and secured important communication routes.

The Mauryan military included infantry, cavalry, chariots and war elephants. These forces required transport, provisions, animal fodder, equipment and supporting workers.

Megasthenes described a committee divided into 6 subcommittees responsible for coordinating military activities.

SubcommitteeArea of responsibility
1Navy
2Transport and provisions
3Infantry or foot soldiers
4Horses and cavalry
5Chariots
6Elephants

The transport and provisions subcommittee had particularly varied responsibilities. It arranged carts and other transport, supplied food for soldiers and fodder for animals, and organised workers who supported military movements.

This description illustrates a central problem of imperial warfare: an army could not operate simply by possessing soldiers and weapons. It also required an organised system for moving and supplying them.

Roads, rivers and political integration

Control over routes was essential to maintaining a geographically extensive empire.

Roads allowed officials and military forces to move between major political centres. Rivers provided important routes for moving goods, particularly in the fertile Gangetic region.

Communication and military protection helped connect distant regions to imperial authority. These arrangements also supported trade and the movement of agricultural and other products.

Political integration did not eliminate regional diversity

The Mauryan Empire brought many territories under the authority of one ruling dynasty. This represented a major development in political integration.

However, the populations of the empire spoke different languages, followed different customs and engaged in different occupations. Its regions also differed greatly in terrain and economic resources.

Consequently, imperial unity did not require every region to possess exactly the same administrative practices.

Prelims focus

  • Direct Mauryan administration was strongest around Pataliputra and major political centres.
  • Royal princes were often appointed to provincial responsibilities.
  • Officials collected taxes and enforced royal instructions.
  • Megasthenes described 6 military subcommittees.
  • Transport and provisions formed a distinct military responsibility.
  • Trap: A large imperial territory did not necessarily have uniform administrative control or identical taxation everywhere.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 6, printed p. 59, and Chapter 8, printed pp. 77–78; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, section 3.2, Administering the Empire, printed pp. 32–35.]

pictures.alt: Mauryan soldiers, ox carts and pack animals travel beside a river as workers organise food and fodder and load supply boats.
pictures.caption: Military movement depended on transport, food, animal fodder and protected communication routes.

pictures.alt: Megasthenes’ 6 military subcommittees: 5 military arms and a separate transport and provisions function covering carts, soldier food, animal fodder and workers.
pictures.caption: The 6 military subcommittees described by Megasthenes.

title: How the Mauryan Empire Functioned: Administration, Revenue and Military Organisation

body:
Ashoka inherited an established empire

Ashoka was the son of Bindusara and grandson of Chandragupta Maurya. He became the third major ruler of the Mauryan dynasty and ruled during the 3rd century BCE.

His reign is commonly dated to approximately 268–232 BCE, although ancient chronologies distinguish accession and formal coronation and the precise dates differ slightly between historical reconstructions.

Ashoka inherited a large empire with its capital at Pataliputra, important provincial centres and established military and administrative arrangements.

The conquest of Kalinga

Kalinga was an important region on the eastern coast of India, principally associated with present-day coastal Odisha.

Ashoka conquered Kalinga in the 8th year after his coronation, conventionally placed around 261 BCE.

The conquest brought Kalinga under Mauryan authority and extended the empire's control over an important eastern coastal region.

However, the war was associated with enormous loss of life and the displacement of people. Ashoka himself described these consequences in Major Rock Edict XIII.

What Major Rock Edict XIII records

According to the figures recorded in Ashoka's inscription:

  • 150,000 people were carried away from Kalinga.
  • 100,000 people were killed.
  • Many times that number died from other causes associated with the conquest.

These are figures stated in the royal inscription, not independently verified modern population statistics. Their importance is that the ruler publicly acknowledged the extensive human suffering caused by his conquest.

Ashoka also expressed distress over the suffering of families, religious communities and people who had lost relatives and companions.

From military conquest to dhamma-vijaya

The Kalinga war became an important turning point in Ashoka's stated approach to conquest.

He increasingly emphasised dhamma-vijaya, meaning conquest through dhamma or moral influence, rather than territorial expansion through military force.

In Major Rock Edict XIII, Ashoka described the suffering caused by war and expressed a preference for winning people through dhamma.

He also advised his descendants to avoid new military conquests or, if military action occurred, to exercise restraint.

What changed, and what did not

Ashoka's expression of remorse did not mean that Kalinga ceased to be part of the empire or that the Mauryan state abolished its army. His own inscription continued to recognise royal authority and the possibility of punishment, including in dealings with forest peoples.

The supported distinction is a change in Ashoka's publicly expressed ideal of conquest, not proof that every form of state coercion disappeared.

Dhamma as a means of political and social integration

The Mauryan Empire contained populations with different customs, languages and religious traditions. Ashoka's dhamma promoted principles intended to be understood across these differences.

Its major teachings included:

  • Respect for parents and elders.
  • Kind treatment of servants and dependants.
  • Compassion towards living beings.
  • Generosity towards Brahmanas and ascetics.
  • Respect for different religious traditions.
  • Restraint in harmful conduct.

Ashoka's dhamma was not simply another name for Buddhism. Although Ashoka was influenced by Buddhist teachings, the public principles of dhamma addressed broader questions of social conduct and coexistence within the empire.

How Ashoka communicated his policy

Ashoka used rock and pillar inscriptions to communicate instructions and moral principles to officials and subjects in different regions.

Most of his inscriptions were written in Prakrit using the Brahmi script. Some inscriptions in the north-west used Kharosthi, while Greek and Aramaic were used in inscriptions associated with Afghanistan.

Special officers called dhamma mahamattas were appointed to promote dhamma among the people.

In this way, Ashoka combined established imperial administration with a programme of moral instruction addressed to diverse populations.

Influence beyond the empire

Ashoka's inscriptions also refer to the spread of dhamma beyond his political frontiers, including towards Hellenistic kingdoms and southern territories such as those of the Cholas and Pandyas.

These statements concern the extension of moral influence and diplomatic communication. They should not automatically be interpreted as claims that every neighbouring kingdom had been militarily conquered.

Prelims focus

  • Ashoka was the son of Bindusara and grandson of Chandragupta Maurya.
  • Kalinga was associated with present-day coastal Odisha.
  • The Kalinga conquest occurred in the 8th year after Ashoka's coronation, conventionally around 261 BCE.
  • Major Rock Edict XIII records the conquest and Ashoka's remorse.
  • The inscription records 150,000 deported and 100,000 killed, with many more deaths.
  • Trap: Dhamma-vijaya did not mean that every neighbouring kingdom became a Mauryan province or that the state abandoned all coercive power.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed pp. 79–81; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed pp. 32–35; Ashoka, Major Rock Edicts II, V and XIII, English translation by S. Dhammika, Livius.org, Ashoka's Rock Edicts, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Ashoka's conquest of Kalinga leads to an inscription reporting human losses, expressing remorse and preferring dhamma-vijaya; the figures are royal claims.
pictures.caption: The conquest of Kalinga was followed by Ashoka's public expression of remorse.

pictures.alt: Kalinga came under Mauryan authority; dhamma-vijaya meant moral influence, not annexation of neighbours such as the Cholas and Pandyas.
pictures.caption: Military annexation and dhamma-vijaya were different forms of extending influence.

title: Ashoka and Kalinga: Military Conquest and the Shift towards Dhamma
